transcript.content: Hello, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose I'm here because things have been pretty stressful at work lately. I work as an interpreter and translator, mostly handling technical and legal documents. Actually, I was just reading an article this morning about how machine translation is supposedly going to replace all of us in the industry, which is just ridiculous. I mean, a computer doesn't understand cultural context, right? When I was doing my graduate degree, I spent an entire semester just analyzing the translation of idioms in post-war European cinema. You just can't automate that kind of nuance, it requires a human touch. 

But, um... anyway, the real issue, the reason I actually made the appointment, is that for months now, I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in our project files. Certain subcontractors and this one colleague of mine keep making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. It's all designed so it looks like my quality control failed. I even brought it up to IT, and they tell me the audit trail is clean, but... I know the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. It’s exactly like when my older brother tried to convince my parents I backed into the mailbox back in high school—he completely staged the whole thing just to get me grounded. People will go to great lengths to cover their tracks, you know? So, yeah, that's what's been going on.
Have you ever considered that these concerns might be mistaken or that there could be another explanation?

Mistaken? Well, sure, I mean, anyone can make a mistake. Human error is a very real thing in my line of work. Like, a few years ago, I was translating this massive contract for a logistics firm in Munich, and I almost used the wrong legal term for 'freight forwarder.' I caught it before delivery, thank god, but it happens. Munich is actually incredible in the fall, by the way. I went there for Oktoberfest back in... 2008, I think? The architecture around the Marienplatz is just stunning, you can spend hours just looking at the Glockenspiel and the tourists... 

But, um... no, with this situation at the office? I'm definitely not mistaken. Like I was just saying a minute ago, I've been watching this happen for months. It's a very deliberate pattern. That colleague and those subcontractors are going into the translation memory and tweaking those timestamps specifically to make my quality control look like it's failing. And I know IT told me the audit trail is perfectly clean—I mentioned that—but honestly, that just proves my point. They’ve arranged the digital record perfectly so that when the fallout happens, all the blame lands squarely on me.
Do you generally avoid jobs or activities because you worry people will criticize or reject you?

Avoid jobs? No, no, I don't do that. I'm actually very confident in my skills, so I don't really worry about people criticizing me or rejecting me. If anything, I take on the complex assignments because I know I can handle the pressure. 

Like, just a few months ago, I took this simultaneous interpreting gig for a renewable energy summit in Oslo. Simultaneous is exhausting—you're in the booth, listening and speaking at the exact same time—but Oslo is just fantastic. Have you ever been? The seafood is incredible. I had this smoked salmon at a little cafe near the waterfront that honestly changed my life. They cure it with dill and juniper berries, I think. I actually tried to recreate the recipe when I got back home, but I couldn't find the right kind of wood chips for my smoker. I bought this electric smoker during the pandemic, thinking I'd get really into barbecue, but honestly, it mostly just takes up space on my patio now. My neighbor keeps complaining about the smell whenever I do use it, which is just absurd because he's the one who leaves his garbage bins out for three days after collection, but... well, anyway. 

Wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, avoiding things. No, I don't avoid work or worry about rejection. I just do my job, and I do it well. It's just the sabotage with the files I have to worry about, not my actual ability to do the work.
Have you felt this kind of suspicion toward other people for most of your adult life?

Most of my adult life? No, no, definitely not. I've never been the type to just go around suspecting people. Honestly, I've always been pretty trusting. Like, when I first moved into my own apartment during grad school, I had this roommate, Greg, who I just met off a campus bulletin board. He was studying marine biology, and I completely trusted him with my half of the rent and everything right from the start. 

We actually had this huge saltwater aquarium in the living room. Keeping a saltwater tank is incredibly difficult, by the way. You have to monitor the salinity and the pH levels constantly. We had these clownfish, and they require a very specific environment to thrive. I remember driving three hours one weekend just to get this specific type of live rock for the tank from a specialty dealer out on the coast. Have you ever driven up the coast highway? It’s absolutely beautiful, especially in the spring when the lupines are blooming everywhere along the cliffs. I used to take my old Subaru out there all the time, just roll the windows down and listen to jazz. I loved that car... the transmission finally gave out at like 150,000 miles, which was a real tragedy. I ended up selling it for parts to this guy who restored vintage wagons. 

But, um... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being suspicious. No, I don't have a history of that at all. It's just this current situation at the office, because, like I said, the evidence with the timestamps is right there. I'm only pointing out what's actually happening.
Have you had any experiences of hearing or seeing things that other people around you do not?

Hearing or seeing things? No, definitely not. I mean, my eyesight isn't what it used to be, I'll admit that. I finally had to get bifocals last year, which was a real blow to the ego, let me tell you. I went to this optometrist downtown, Dr. Lin, and she has this amazing antique collection of spectacles in her waiting room. Like, actual pince-nez glasses from the 1800s. It’s fascinating how they used to make them with real tortoiseshell. 

I actually read this whole book on the history of optics after that appointment. Did you know that the first wearable glasses were invented in Italy around the 13th century? They didn't even have arms that went over the ears back then, they just balanced them on the bridge of the nose. It must have been so annoying to keep them from falling off every time you looked down to read a manuscript. I translate a lot of historical documents sometimes, and I always wonder how those monks managed it by candlelight. Candles give off such terrible light for reading. I bought these beeswax candles from a farmer's market a few weeks ago—supposedly they burn cleaner—but they just made my whole living room smell like honey and smoke. 

But anyway, no, I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. I'm perfectly grounded in reality. It's just the very real tampering with my files that I'm dealing with.
Have you generally had trouble trusting other people for most of your adult life?

Trouble trusting people? No, I wouldn't say that. Like I said before, I've always been pretty open and trusting with people. I mean, you have to be in my line of work, right? When you're interpreting for two parties, you're the bridge between them. You have to trust that they're communicating in good faith, and they have to trust you to convey the nuances. Nuance is everything in translation. 

I was actually reading this article the other day about how machine translation is getting better, but it still completely misses cultural idioms. Like, you can't just literally translate "kick the bucket" into French and expect it to make sense. It's fascinating, really. I started collecting these idioms from different languages in a notebook. I have this beautiful leather-bound journal I bought in Florence a few years ago. Florence is incredible—the architecture, the art. I spent a whole afternoon just staring at the doors of the Baptistery. Ghiberti's "Gates of Paradise," they call them. The bronze work is just breathtaking. I took so many photos, but I lost my phone on the train back to Rome, which was a nightmare. Trying to navigate the Italian railway system without a phone... well, let's just say I got very familiar with the local bus routes instead.

But, um... sorry, what was the question? Trusting people? Yeah, no, I don't have a problem trusting people generally. It's just this specific situation at work. When the proof is right there in the file history, you can't just ignore it, you know? But overall, no, I'm not an untrusting person.
Have you ever had beliefs or experiences that other people would think are unusual or odd, but that you felt were meaningful or true?

Unusual beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, what even counts as unusual these days? Everyone has their own way of looking at the world. Like, my neighbor, he's absolutely convinced that planting his tomatoes according to the phases of the moon makes them taste better. I don't know if I buy into that, but his tomatoes are fantastic. 

I actually tried growing my own heirloom tomatoes last summer on my balcony. I got these seeds from a catalog, "Brandywines," they're called. They're supposed to be incredibly flavorful, but they are so finicky. You have to make sure they get exactly the right amount of sunlight, but not too much direct afternoon heat or the leaves scorch. I ended up building this elaborate little shade structure out of bamboo poles and some old linen curtains I found at a thrift store. That thrift store is amazing, by the way. It's run by this charity that supports retired greyhounds. Have you ever met a greyhound? They are the gentlest dogs. They call them "45-mile-per-hour couch potatoes" because they just want to sprint for ten minutes and then sleep for the rest of the day. I almost adopted one a few years ago, this beautiful brindle female named Daisy, but my apartment complex had a strict weight limit on pets, which is so arbitrary if you ask me. A big, lazy dog is way quieter than a yappy little terrier. 

Wait, sorry, I'm rambling again. What were you asking? Unusual beliefs? No, nothing like that. I'm a very logical person. I deal in facts and accurate translations. That's why this whole thing with the timestamps at the office is so frustrating, because the facts are right there in front of everyone, but they just refuse to see it. But no, I don't have any weird or odd beliefs.
Do you feel close to other people, or do you usually prefer to keep your distance?

Close to people? Oh, yeah, definitely. I mean, I have a solid group of friends, and I'm pretty close with my sister. We actually try to do a video call every Sunday evening. She lives in Seattle now, which is such a beautiful city, but man, it rains a lot. I went to visit her last October, and it just drizzled for four days straight. We still had a good time, though. We went to Pike Place Market, and I finally got to see those guys throwing the fish. It's quite a spectacle. 

We actually bought some fresh salmon while we were there and took it back to her place to grill. She has this amazing cedar plank grilling set she got for her birthday. Have you ever had cedar plank salmon? It completely changes the flavor profile, gives it this incredible smoky, earthy taste. I tried to replicate it when I got back home, but I bought the wrong kind of wood planks at the hardware store—pine, I think—and it just made the fish taste like floor cleaner. It was a disaster. I had to throw the whole thing out and order pizza instead. I ended up getting a pie from that place on 4th Street, the one with the really authentic Neapolitan crust. They import their flour directly from Italy, which makes all the difference in the dough. You really can't cut corners on the ingredients if you want a proper pizza.

But, um, anyway, yeah, I feel close to people. I don't keep my distance or anything. I've always been pretty social, which is why it's so strange that my coworkers are suddenly acting so guarded around me lately, ever since I brought up the file discrepancies. But generally, no, I like being around people.
Outside of the situation at work, do you often suspect that other people may be trying to harm, deceive, or take advantage of you?

Harm or deceive me? No, definitely not. I mean, outside of the office, my life is pretty normal and quiet. I don't walk around thinking people are out to get me or anything like that. 

Well, I mean, except for those spam callers, right? The ones who leave those automated voicemails saying your car warranty is expiring or that you owe back taxes. They're definitely trying to deceive people. I got three of those calls just yesterday. It's ridiculous, especially since I don't even own a car right now! I sold my Honda Civic back in 2018 because the public transit in my neighborhood got so much better when they extended the light rail. Have you ridden the new green line yet? It is so clean, and they have these huge windows. I love taking it downtown just to look at the architecture. 

I actually took it down to the arts district last weekend because there was this estate sale I wanted to check out. I've started collecting vintage typewriters—well, I say collecting, but I only have two so far, an Underwood and a Smith Corona. The mechanical sound they make is just so satisfying, you know? Clack, clack, clack, and then the little *ding* at the end of the line. It really makes you feel like you're actually writing something important, unlike typing on a smooth glass screen where everything is just deleted with a backspace. I spent three hours on Saturday just cleaning the keys on the Underwood with a Q-tip and some rubbing alcohol. The ribbon is completely dried out, though, so I need to find a place that still sells replacements. I read on a forum that there's a guy in Oregon who still manufactures them using the original ink formulas from the 1950s. 

But, um... wait, what was the question? Oh, right, people trying to take advantage of me. No, no. Other than the occasional telemarketer, I don't worry about that at all. People in my day-to-day life are fine. It's really just that specific situation at work with the file timestamps that I have to keep my guard up about.
Have you ever been this suspicious of people before this current problem at work?

Suspicious? No, not really. I've never been the type to be overly suspicious of people. I usually take people at their word. I mean, trust is important, right? It's the foundation of any good relationship, whether it's personal or professional. 

Speaking of professional relationships, I used to work with this guy, David, at my old translation agency. He was such a character. He always wore these incredibly loud, patterned ties—like, neon geometric shapes or little cartoon penguins. He said they helped him stay awake during long document reviews. We were working on this massive legal translation project once, a huge corporate merger, and the documents were just endless. Pages and pages of legalese in German. German is such a fascinating language, the way they can just compound words together to create entirely new concepts. Like *Schadenfreude*, right? Everyone knows that one. But there's also *Kummerspeck*, which literally translates to "grief bacon," meaning the weight you gain from emotional overeating. I just love that. It's so descriptive. 

I actually started baking my own bread during that project because I needed a hobby that involved working with my hands to offset all the mental strain. Sourdough, specifically. It's a real commitment, keeping the starter alive. You have to feed it every day, like a pet. I named mine "Dough-lores." I got really into scoring the top of the loaves before baking, making these intricate wheat stalk patterns with a razor blade. It's surprisingly therapeutic. 

But, uh, anyway, to answer your question... no, I haven't ever been this suspicious before. This whole thing with the timestamps is completely new territory for me. It's just so glaringly obvious that something isn't right there, but before this, no, I've always been pretty trusting.
Before this work problem started, had you ever strongly believed that other people were deliberately trying to trick or harm you?

Trick or harm me? No, I don't think so. I mean, I'm trying to think back, but nothing really comes to mind. Like I said, I've always been a pretty trusting guy. 

I did have this one neighbor, Mrs. Gable, when I lived in my old apartment complex on 8th Avenue. I swear she used to steal my Sunday newspaper, but that's not really tricking or harming me, just being annoying. She had this tiny little Pomeranian that barked at absolutely everything. A leaf blows across the sidewalk? Bark. The mail carrier drops off a package? Bark. I don't know how she stood it. I've always been more of a cat person, myself. They're so much quieter and more independent. 

I adopted a rescue cat a few years ago, a tabby named Barnaby. He has this funny little quirk where he'll only drink water if it's moving, so I had to buy him one of those little fountain bowls. It has a little flower in the middle where the water bubbles up. It's actually quite soothing to listen to, like a tiny indoor brook. I put it right next to my collection of peace lilies. I've been trying to propagate them, which is surprisingly easy. You just divide the root ball when you repot them. I've given away like five baby peace lilies to friends this year. They make great housewarming gifts because they're almost impossible to kill. 

But, um, anyway, what were we talking about? Oh, right, people tricking me before the work thing. No, no, nothing like that. Just the usual stuff, like Mrs. Gable and the newspaper. Nothing serious like what's happening at the agency.
Do you ever have similar suspicions that people are trying to harm or deceive you in other parts of your life, outside of work?

Wait, didn't you just ask me that? Or something really similar? But no, like I said, outside of work, everything is fine. I don't think anyone is trying to harm me or deceive me in my personal life. 

It's really just a quiet life, you know? Just me and Barnaby, and my typewriters, and my sourdough starter. Actually, I was thinking about trying to make a rye bread this weekend. I've been reading up on it, and apparently, rye flour behaves really differently than wheat flour because it has less gluten. You have to handle it differently, or it turns out like a brick. I found this recipe in an old cookbook I picked up at a thrift store—it was one of those community cookbooks put together by a church group in the 1970s. Those are always the best because the recipes are tried and true, you know? Real family staples. There was one recipe in there for a Jell-O salad with carrots and pineapple in it, which just sounds absolutely horrifying to me. The 70s were a weird time for food, weren't they? Everything was either suspended in gelatin or covered in a thick cream sauce. 

But anyway, sorry, I'm rambling again. No, I don't have those kinds of suspicions outside of the office. It's strictly related to those file timestamps at work.
Have you ever found clear evidence that the file tampering was actually happening?

Evidence? Yes, of course. I mean, I'm here because for months I've been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It's so specific. Certain subcontractors, and this one colleague in particular, they keep making these tiny, almost imperceptible changes to the translation memory. And the timestamps, they alter them just enough so it looks like my quality control failed. 

It's meticulous work, really, modifying a translation memory database. You have to understand the underlying XML structure, which most translators don't even bother to look at. They just use the interface. But if you open the raw file in a text editor, you can see all the tags. It reminds me of when I tried to learn HTML back in the late 90s. Everyone was making their own personal websites on GeoCities, remember that? I had one dedicated entirely to vintage typewriter restoration. I had these awful animated GIFs of gears turning, and MIDI music playing in the background. I think it was a MIDI version of "The Entertainer." It took forever to load on dial-up. You'd sit there listening to the modem screeching, just waiting for a pixelated picture of an Underwood No. 5 to appear. 

I actually just found an Underwood No. 5 at an estate sale last month. The carriage was completely seized up, but I managed to soak it in mineral spirits and get it moving again. The smell of mineral spirits is so strong, though, I had to keep all the windows open, and Barnaby absolutely hated it. He hid under the sofa for two days. 

But anyway, the evidence. Yes. Even when I point out the discrepancies, and IT comes back and says the audit trail is "clean," I know what I'm looking at. I know the record has been deliberately arranged to put the blame on me. They cover their tracks, but the pattern is there if you know how to read it.
Do you believe the same people are also targeting you in ways outside of work?

No, no, they don't care about my life outside the office. Why would they? It's just the translation files. Outside of that whole project issue, everything is perfectly normal. I still do my regular translation work, I manage the team's workflow, I pay my bills on time, keep up with my family routines... I actually just called my sister last night for her birthday. She lives out in Oregon now, near Portland. She keeps trying to convince me to move out there, saying the weather is better for growing my peace lilies, but honestly, it rains so much there. I don't know how people deal with all that dampness. It's terrible for vintage typewriters, too. The moisture just gets right into the mechanisms and rusts everything solid. You'd have to keep a dehumidifier running 24/7 just to protect your collection. 

I was watching this documentary the other day about the Pacific Northwest, and they showed these huge slugs they have out there. Banana slugs, they call them. They're bright yellow and can get to be like ten inches long. Imagine stepping on one of those in the dark when you're just trying to take the trash out. Barnaby would probably try to eat it and make himself sick. 

But, right, sorry, I'm drifting again. No, they aren't targeting me outside of work. The only time things really go off track or get complicated is when those specific file histories or those certain coworkers come up. Everything else in my life is completely fine.
What makes you so sure that your coworker is the one tampering with the files?

Well, it's just obvious when you look at the workflow. He's the only one who has the right access level at the exact times the timestamps are shifted, and he's always the one who reviews that specific batch of translations before they go to final QA. It's a very specific sequence of events. 

Actually, speaking of sequences, I was trying to explain the sequence of events in the French Revolution to my nephew the other day. He's in middle school and he had this huge history project due. He was getting completely overwhelmed by all the different factions—the Jacobins, the Girondins. It is a lot to keep straight, to be fair. I ended up pulling out my old college textbooks to help him. I minored in history, you know. I always thought if the translation thing didn't work out, I could be a historian or an archivist. There's something so satisfying about organizing old documents, preserving them. 

I have this one box of letters I bought at an antique store—they're from a soldier during World War I, writing back to his wife in Ohio. The handwriting is beautiful, this sweeping cursive that nobody uses anymore. I've been slowly transcribing them in my spare time. Sometimes I type them up on my 1932 Royal Quiet De Luxe. That machine has such a crisp pica typeface. It's the same model Hemingway used, actually, though I think he had a slightly later version. 

But, right, the tampering. Yeah, it's just... I know it's him because the timing of the edits aligns perfectly with his shift, and he's the one who stands to benefit if my quality metrics drop. It's just simple deduction.
Have you been this suspicious of people since early adulthood?

No, no, definitely not. This is a recent thing. This has been going on for about 11 months, since shortly after I was put in charge of the new localization project. Before that, everything was fine. I've always gotten along with my coworkers. I mean, I'm a pretty easygoing guy. 

I actually used to organize the office potlucks before the pandemic. I make this incredible baked ziti. The secret is to mix a little bit of ricotta in with the mozzarella, and you have to use fresh basil. Dried basil just doesn't have the same punch. I grow my own basil on the kitchen windowsill. It's right next to the peace lilies. They get just the right amount of morning sun there. 

I tried growing tomatoes once, too, but the squirrels kept getting to them before they were ripe. They would just take one bite out of a green tomato and leave it sitting on the railing. It was infuriating. I even tried sprinkling cayenne pepper around the pots, because I read online that it deters them, but I think it just seasoned their snack. Squirrels are so bold these days. There's this one squirrel in my neighborhood that has a chunk missing from its ear, and I swear it recognizes me. It just sits on the fence and stares at me when I take Barnaby out for his morning walk. Barnaby usually barks at it, but he's a dachshund, so he's not exactly intimidating. He just sort of waddles and yaps. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't always been suspicious. It's just these last 11 months, since that specific project started and I started noticing the file changes. Before that, I never had a reason to doubt anyone's work.
Before these last 11 months, did you often have the same kind of suspicion toward other people?

No, like I was saying, really not at all. If anything, I've always been a bit too trusting before all this project nonsense started. 

I remember back in grad school, I lent my absolute favorite fountain pen to a classmate. It was a vintage Parker 51, aerometric filler, this beautiful cedar blue color. You don't just hand those out to anyone, you know? But I didn't even think twice about it. I just assumed he'd treat it with respect. Of course, he ended up springing the tines on the nib because people who are used to ballpoints always press down way too hard. They treat a 14-karat gold nib like it's a cheap plastic Bic you'd find at a bank. It completely ruined the ink flow. 

I actually had to send it off to a specialized nibsmith in Ohio to get it realigned. It took three months to get it back, and when it finally arrived, the guy had used this lovely dark teal ink to test it. I think it was Diamine Eau de Nil, or maybe Marine. Such a great color for editing documents. It pops off the page but it isn't quite as aggressive as red ink. I always try to use teal or a nice warm sepia when I'm doing hard-copy proofreading for the translation team. Red just feels so adversarial, don't you think? Like a teacher grading a math test. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being suspicious of people. No, definitely not. I've always just taken people at their word until this whole file tampering thing started happening.
When you think back to your teens and twenties, did you generally trust other people, or did you often assume they had hidden motives?

No, I really did trust people back then. I didn't think anyone was out to get me or had hidden motives. Like I said, I was probably too trusting. 

I actually met my best friend in my twenties, during a summer study abroad program in Kyoto. We were both totally lost trying to navigate the subway system on our first day. The maps were incredibly overwhelming if you weren't used to them, all those intersecting, brightly colored lines. It looked like a modern art piece, honestly. Sort of like a Mondrian painting, but with more diagonals. I've always appreciated Mondrian's use of primary colors. It's so stark and structured. 

I tried painting for a little while after I got back from Japan. Mostly watercolors. I loved how unpredictable the medium is, how the water just sort of decides where the pigment is going to settle. I painted this one landscape of the Arashiyama bamboo grove that I was actually quite proud of. I framed it in this beautiful dark walnut frame I found at a flea market. The guy selling it was this old carpenter who told me he used to build sets for the local theater company. He had all these amazing stories about trying to construct a two-story house on stage for a production of *Noises Off*. Have you ever seen that play? The timing required for the physical comedy is just astounding. Doors opening and closing at the exact right millisecond. 

But, yeah, no, I didn't assume people had hidden motives back then. I just took them as they were.
Before these past 11 months, did you generally find yourself suspicious of people in most relationships, like friends, family, or coworkers?

No, really, I've never had issues like that with anyone. Friends, family, coworkers... we all got along perfectly fine. I mean, you kind of have to trust your coworkers in my line of work. 

Like, I used to partner with this guy David for simultaneous interpretation at these big international medical conferences. You have to trust your partner completely in the booth, because you have to switch off every twenty minutes. If you don't, your brain just completely fries. It's incredibly intense work. We did a lot of cardiology conferences together, actually. The terminology is just fascinating. It's amazing how the heart has its own internal electrical system, like a little dedicated power grid. 

Speaking of power grids, I actually had to call an electrician out to the house last Tuesday because the breaker for my kitchen kept tripping every time I ran the microwave and the espresso machine at the same time. Turns out the house still has some of the original wiring from the seventies. The electrician was this really nice guy, though. He wore these vintage leather work boots that he said he’d had re-soled three times. I really appreciate that, you know? Taking care of things instead of just throwing them away. People are so quick to just toss everything into a landfill these days. It’s like we have no respect for craftsmanship anymore. I try to buy things that last, even if they cost a little more upfront. 

But, um... yeah. To your question, no, I wasn't suspicious of anyone in my life before this localization project started. Everything was completely normal.
If someone you trusted showed you clear evidence that the file changes were not being tampered with, would you be able to accept that?

Well, the thing is, I don't know what kind of evidence they could possibly show me, because the proof is already right there. I mean, I’m here because for months I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It’s certain subcontractors and this one specific colleague, and they keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. It’s entirely designed so it looks like my quality control failed. And, look, even when IT says the audit trail is clean, I know the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. IT just runs their standard diagnostic scripts and calls it a day. 

The guy in IT who ran the check, actually, he uses one of those incredibly loud mechanical keyboards. You know the ones? With the Cherry MX Blue switches? It's just a constant, aggressive clicking sound all day long. I honestly don't know how anyone in an open-plan office tolerates it. I actually prefer a Topre switch myself. It's an electrostatic capacitive switch, so it gives you this really satisfying, muted thud instead of a high-pitched click. I imported a specialized keyboard from Tokyo a few years ago just for that reason. 

The shipping took absolutely forever, though, because it got held up in customs in Anchorage for almost three weeks. Have you ever been to Alaska? I've always wanted to take one of those small-ship cruises through Glacier Bay before the ice completely recedes. I saw a documentary on PBS recently about the tufted puffins up there, and their nesting habits are just fascinating. They dig these little burrows in the soil on the edges of cliffs, almost like prairie dogs, which you wouldn't expect from a seabird. Nature is just incredibly adaptable like that, isn't it?

patient.answer:

It just sits on the fence and stares at me when I take Barnaby out for his morning walk. Barnaby usually barks at it, but he's a dachshund, so he's not exactly intimidating. He just sort of waddles and yaps. 

But no, to answer your question, I haven't always been suspicious. It's just these last 11 months, since that specific project started and I started noticing the file changes. Before that, I never had a reason to doubt anyone's work.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the patient’s suspiciousness is part of a longstanding pervasive pattern (paranoid personality disorder) or a recent fixed persecutory delusion (delusional disorder, persecutory type).
doctor.question: Before these last 11 months, did you often have the same kind of suspicion toward other people?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient had similar suspicions toward other people before the last 11 months, which is inquiring about a long-standing personality trait (like Paranoid Personality Disorder) versus a recent onset. While the duration (11 months) was just discussed, there is no specific symptom profile item for the absence of lifelong suspiciousness or paranoid personality traits.

patient.answer:
No, like I was saying, really not at all. If anything, I've always been a bit too trusting before all this project nonsense started. 

I remember back in grad school, I lent my absolute favorite fountain pen to a classmate. It was a vintage Parker 51, aerometric filler, this beautiful cedar blue color. You don't just hand those out to anyone, you know? But I didn't even think twice about it. I just assumed he'd treat it with respect. Of course, he ended up springing the tines on the nib because people who are used to ballpoints always press down way too hard. They treat a 14-karat gold nib like it's a cheap plastic Bic you'd find at a bank. It completely ruined the ink flow. 

I actually had to send it off to a specialized nibsmith in Ohio to get it realigned. It took three months to get it back, and when it finally arrived, the guy had used this lovely dark teal ink to test it. I think it was Diamine Eau de Nil, or maybe Marine. Such a great color for editing documents. It pops off the page but it isn't quite as aggressive as red ink. I always try to use teal or a nice warm sepia when I'm doing hard-copy proofreading for the translation team. Red just feels so adversarial, don't you think? Like a teacher grading a math test. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, being suspicious of people. No, definitely not. I've always just taken people at their word until this whole file tampering thing started happening.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the patient has a pervasive, long-standing pattern of suspiciousness (paranoid personality disorder) rather than a recent fixed delusion limited to one context.
doctor.question: When you think back to your teens and twenties, did you generally trust other people, or did you often assume they had hidden motives?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my general personality and level of trust/suspicion during my teens and twenties (checking for lifelong paranoid personality traits). None of my symptom profile items cover my personality traits in my teens and twenties; they only cover the 11-month duration of the delusion, the delusion itself, and my functioning.

patient.answer:
No, I really did trust people back then. I didn't think anyone was out to get me or had hidden motives. Like I said, I was probably too trusting. 

I actually met my best friend in my twenties, during a summer study abroad program in Kyoto. We were both totally lost trying to navigate the subway system on our first day. The maps were incredibly overwhelming if you weren't used to them, all those intersecting, brightly colored lines. It looked like a modern art piece, honestly. Sort of like a Mondrian painting, but with more diagonals. I've always appreciated Mondrian's use of primary colors. It's so stark and structured. 

I tried painting for a little while after I got back from Japan. Mostly watercolors. I loved how unpredictable the medium is, how the water just sort of decides where the pigment is going to settle. I painted this one landscape of the Arashiyama bamboo grove that I was actually quite proud of. I framed it in this beautiful dark walnut frame I found at a flea market. The guy selling it was this old carpenter who told me he used to build sets for the local theater company. He had all these amazing stories about trying to construct a two-story house on stage for a production of *Noises Off*. Have you ever seen that play? The timing required for the physical comedy is just astounding. Doors opening and closing at the exact right millisecond. 

But, yeah, no, I didn't assume people had hidden motives back then. I just took them as they were.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the patient has a long-standing pattern of distrust and suspiciousness across many relationships, which would support paranoid personality disorder rather than a more recent delusional disorder.
doctor.question: Before these past 11 months, did you generally find yourself suspicious of people in most relationships, like friends, family, or coworkers?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about a history of pervasive suspiciousness (which relates to Paranoid Personality Disorder). The patient's symptom profile covers Delusions, Additional Requirement 1 (functioning not markedly impaired), Functional Impairment, and Duration (11 months). It does not have an item for a lifelong history of pervasive suspiciousness.

patient.answer:
No, really, I've never had issues like that with anyone. Friends, family, coworkers... we all got along perfectly fine. I mean, you kind of have to trust your coworkers in my line of work. 

Like, I used to partner with this guy David for simultaneous interpretation at these big international medical conferences. You have to trust your partner completely in the booth, because you have to switch off every twenty minutes. If you don't, your brain just completely fries. It's incredibly intense work. We did a lot of cardiology conferences together, actually. The terminology is just fascinating. It's amazing how the heart has its own internal electrical system, like a little dedicated power grid. 

Speaking of power grids, I actually had to call an electrician out to the house last Tuesday because the breaker for my kitchen kept tripping every time I ran the microwave and the espresso machine at the same time. Turns out the house still has some of the original wiring from the seventies. The electrician was this really nice guy, though. He wore these vintage leather work boots that he said he’d had re-soled three times. I really appreciate that, you know? Taking care of things instead of just throwing them away. People are so quick to just toss everything into a landfill these days. It’s like we have no respect for craftsmanship anymore. I try to buy things that last, even if they cost a little more upfront. 

But, um... yeah. To your question, no, I wasn't suspicious of anyone in my life before this localization project started. Everything was completely normal.

doctor.intent: Assess whether the belief is fixed despite contrary evidence, which helps distinguish a delusional disorder from a longstanding personality pattern.
doctor.question: If someone you trusted showed you clear evidence that the file changes were not being tampered with, would you be able to accept that?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for months I’ve been seeing the same pattern in the project files—certain subcontractors and one colleague keep making tiny changes to the translation memory and timestamps so it looks like my quality control failed, and even when IT says the audit trail is clean, I know the record has been arranged to put the blame on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient's beliefs are fixed and resistant to contradictory evidence ('If someone you trusted showed you clear evidence... would you be able to accept that?'), which directly maps to the 'Delusions' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, the thing is, I don't know what kind of evidence they could possibly show me, because the proof is already right there. I mean, I’m here because for months I’ve been seeing the exact same pattern in the project files. It’s certain subcontractors and this one specific colleague, and they keep making these tiny, deliberate changes to the translation memory and the timestamps. It’s entirely designed so it looks like my quality control failed. And, look, even when IT says the audit trail is clean, I know the record has been arranged to put the blame on me. IT just runs their standard diagnostic scripts and calls it a day. 

The guy in IT who ran the check, actually, he uses one of those incredibly loud mechanical keyboards. You know the ones? With the Cherry MX Blue switches? It's just a constant, aggressive clicking sound all day long. I honestly don't know how anyone in an open-plan office tolerates it. I actually prefer a Topre switch myself. It's an electrostatic capacitive switch, so it gives you this really satisfying, muted thud instead of a high-pitched click. I imported a specialized keyboard from Tokyo a few years ago just for that reason. 

The shipping took absolutely forever, though, because it got held up in customs in Anchorage for almost three weeks. Have you ever been to Alaska? I've always wanted to take one of those small-ship cruises through Glacier Bay before the ice completely recedes. I saw a documentary on PBS recently about the tufted puffins up there, and their nesting habits are just fascinating. They dig these little burrows in the soil on the edges of cliffs, almost like prairie dogs, which you wouldn't expect from a seabird. Nature is just incredibly adaptable like that, isn't it?
